Examples & Exercises

Draw the best-response correspondences of the Stag Hunt game and show there are three Nash equilibria (two pure, one mixed).

u1(S,q)=4q,u1(H,q)=3u_1(S,q) = 4q, \quad u_1(H,q) = 3u1​(S,q)=4q,u1​(H,q)=3
q∗=3/4,p∗=3/4q^* = 3/4, \quad p^* = 3/4q∗=3/4,p∗=3/4
Show proof
  1. Player 1: u1(S,q)=4qu_1(S, q) = 4qu1​(S,q)=4q, u1(H,q)=3q+3(1−q)=3u_1(H, q) = 3q + 3(1-q) = 3u1​(H,q)=3q+3(1−q)=3. From 4q=34q = 34q=3, q∗=3/4q^* = 3/4q∗=3/4: HHH is best for q<3/4q < 3/4q<3/4, SSS for q>3/4q > 3/4q>3/4. By symmetry player 2's indifference point is p∗=3/4p^* = 3/4p∗=3/4.
  2. Intersections: (q,p)=(0,0)(q,p) = (0,0)(q,p)=(0,0) i.e. (H,H)(H,H)(H,H), (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) i.e. (S,S)(S,S)(S,S), and the fully mixed (3/4,3/4)(3/4, 3/4)(3/4,3/4). At each, the correspondences "hold" each other — no unilateral deviation pays.

Show Matching Pennies has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium and its unique equilibrium is (p∗,q∗)=(1/2,1/2)(p^*, q^*) = (1/2, 1/2)(p∗,q∗)=(1/2,1/2).

BR1(q)={1q>1/2[0,1]q=1/20q<1/2BR_1(q) = \begin{cases} 1 & q > 1/2 \\ [0,1] & q = 1/2 \\ 0 & q < 1/2 \end{cases}BR1​(q)=⎩⎨⎧​1[0,1]0​q>1/2q=1/2q<1/2​
Show proof
  1. Check the four cells: at (H,H)(H,H)(H,H) player 2 wants TTT (1>−11 > -11>−1); at (H,T)(H,T)(H,T) player 1 wants TTT; at (T,H)(T,H)(T,H) player 1 wants HHH; at (T,T)(T,T)(T,T) player 2 wants HHH. No cell is a mutual best response.
  2. In mixtures, u1(H,q)=2q−1u_1(H,q) = 2q-1u1​(H,q)=2q−1 and u1(T,q)=1−2qu_1(T,q) = 1-2qu1​(T,q)=1−2q give q∗=1/2q^* = 1/2q∗=1/2, and symmetrically p∗=1/2p^* = 1/2p∗=1/2. In the correspondence diagram the two step functions cross exactly once, at (1/2,1/2)(1/2, 1/2)(1/2,1/2) — the unique Nash equilibrium.
